extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in philosophy of mathematics; philosophers interested in naturalism and related epistemological/ontological debates
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating naturalism in philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing the criteria, arguments, and standards offered for defending or criticizing methodological, heterogeneous, and ontological forms of naturalism as they apply to mathematics and the philosophy of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks of a discipline's success
rubrics_metrics.description: Rough marks of a discipline’s success: (i) among its practitioners there is a widely shared conception of the discipline’s guiding questions and permissible methodology; and (ii) there is progress within the discipline in addressing its guiding questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that scientific or mathematical standards are the most successful we possess, but subject to relativism: if success is judged purely by S-standards then self-supporting but intuitively unacceptable standards (e.g., 'Guru-ology') may count as successful. Thus success-as-standard needs a non-question-begging, naturalistically acceptable account of 'success'. Also, success in one sphere may not transfer to another (e.g., biology’s success does not automatically give it authority in mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Success measured by explanation/prediction of natural phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Success might be measured by how well the standards explain and predict natural phenomena — i.e., how they cope with the subject matter of natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This seems question-begging for scientific naturalism because it uses scientific standards to measure success; analogous non-scientific standards (e.g., 'astrological phenomena' judged by astrologers) could self-vindicate. A naturalistically acceptable, non-question-begging account of 'success' must be found for this criterion to support naturalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement / Community consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad agreement or consensus within a discipline is taken as evidence that its standards are preferable (science/mathematics often reach broad agreement compared to traditional philosophy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement is a contingent social fact and can result from non-epistemic forces (e.g., coercion); thus what matters is the explanation of why agreement obtains. More refined versions focus on tractability of disagreement rather than mere presence of agreement. Be wary of mistaking contingent consensus for epistemic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tractability of disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: A discipline's disagreements may be more 'tractable' (resolvable in principle) than another's; tractability of dispute resolution supports treating its standards as more truth-conducive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments about tractability often rely on highly idealized subjects with greater factual/logical knowledge — this risks question-begging (e.g., theological anti-naturalists could posit ideal subjects informed about supernatural facts). Also, tractability need not show transferability of standards across different subject-matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical success / Track Record Argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The superior historical track record of scientific and mathematical standards (their past success) gives them epistemic authority over other standards; used as an argument for global naturalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms include: the No Dogmatism objection (past failures don't compel rejection of a method; science itself eschews certainty), and the Schools objection (philosophers belong to traditions/schools that interpret history non-pejoratively, undermining the Track Record). Additionally, past success in one sphere doesn't necessarily warrant authority in another; examples: Popperian standards once led to mistaken philosophical views but that doesn't refute other philosophers' standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Dogmatism and Schools objections (to Track Record Argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections showing that historical failures don't logically force rejection of a method (No Dogmatism) and that philosophers' affiliation to schools weakens claims that philosophy has uniformly poor track record (Schools objection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These function as scoring/defeater conditions for the Track Record Argument: they reduce its force because historical assessment is mediated by interpretive traditions and because science disallows absolute trust in any single method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy thesis (mathematics methodologically autonomous)
rubrics_metrics.description: The thesis that mathematics is autonomous: traditionally scientific or philosophical arguments do not enter into the justification of mathematical statements; mathematical justification is determined by internal, mathematical reasons (proof, axiomatic method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maddy defends this by appeal to cases (e.g., the fate of definabilism regarding Axiom of Choice) and internal maxims like MAXIMIZE and UNIFY. Criticisms note that philosophical doctrine can inspire practice, maxims may be underpinned by philosophical stances (e.g., realism), and distinguishing justification from inspiration is difficult. Evaluating the autonomy thesis requires clarifying the boundary between justification vs inspiration and identifying justificationally operative factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal mathematical maxims as methodological criteria (e.g., MAXIMIZE, UNIFY)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice is guided by internal methodological maxims such as MAXIMIZE (favoring expansive universes of sets) and UNIFY (foundation-building ambition of set theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maddy treats these as purely internal to mathematics and not underlain by philosophical beliefs; critics argue these maxims may subtly rely on philosophical commitments (e.g., realism) and require justificational scrutiny. Examples: MAXIMIZE favors forcing axioms; UNIFY relates to set theory's foundational aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneous naturalism (bivalent standards depending on question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt mathematical standards for mathematics-proper (e.g., which axioms to accept) and scientific standards for the philosophy of mathematics and other philosophical questions (e.g., interpretation of mathematical theories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maddy's 'Second Philosophy' advocates this bivalent stance; it implies that when mathematical practice sanctions a theory (e.g., ZFC+LCA), philosophy must defer on mathematical questions but may apply scientific criteria for interpretive/philosophical issues. Critics highlight a potential inconsistency: endorsing mathematical practice as authoritative for acceptance while using scientific standards to adjudicate truth/interpretation may be incoherent unless 'acceptance' is decoupled from truth-commitment (a move that risks collapsing into scientific naturalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arealism / Enhanced if-thenism (mathematics as means-ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that pure mathematics is not in the business of establishing truth but of using if-then frameworks; mathematicians select 'ifs' (axioms) and pursue means-ends rationales (preferences, mathematical goals) rather than truth claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maddy's Arealism and later 'Enhanced if-thenism' construe selection of axioms as preference-driven but rational in terms of facilitating mathematical goals; critics (e.g., Leng) argue that indispensability in empirical science can secure objectivity of mathematical concepts and challenge claims that only practice uncovers depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological naturalism (natural-scientific arbiter of ontology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ontological naturalism: the ontology of mathematics should be that of our best natural science (only entities posited by natural sciences exist) or, on a stronger reading, only spatiotemporal entities exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quinean/Putnam-inspired scientific platonists use scientific ontology to argue for mathematical platonism; the approach raises problems because scientific theories concern contingent, spatiotemporal entities whereas mathematical entities are typically treated as necessary/abstract. Debates center on whether scientific methods can legitimately settle mathematical ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory / Enhanced Indispensability Argument
rubrics_metrics.description: All entities indispensable to our best scientific explanations should be included in ontology; explanatory indispensability is used to argue that mathematical objects should be ontologically posited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed and defended in various forms (Colyvan, Bangu 'posit realism'); opposed by nominalists and critics (Field, Sober, Maddy, Roland) who argue against naturalising mathematical ontology via indispensability. Applicability depends on whether mathematical entities truly play explanatory roles and whether explanation is a reliable guide to ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatiotemporal cardinality constraint (cardinality problem for reductionism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reductionist ontological naturalism faces a cardinality problem: there appear to be far fewer spatiotemporal entities than required to interpret set theory literally or non-vacuously, so spacetime cannot supply models for full set theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields worries: (i) not enough spatiotemporal entities to account for set-theoretic universe; (ii) if spacetime were large enough, the truth of set theory would be contingent on our universe's features, conflicting with mathematical necessity. These operate as strong objections to reductionist ontological naturalism (see Paseau).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrariness problem for reductionism
rubrics_metrics.description: If arithmetic or other branches of mathematics are about particular spatiotemporal entities, it is arbitrary which concrete objects are assigned numbers (e.g., which spatiotemporal entity is zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benacerraf-style objection: reductionism faces charges of arbitrariness about theoretical identifications; reductionists respond by treating identifications as theoretical proposals rather than meaning-claims, but the objection highlights a substantial cost for spatiotemporal reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict with mathematical method (empirical mismatch objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: If mathematical objects were spatiotemporal, mathematicians would be expected to run experiments to discover their properties; the absence of such empirical methods in mathematics suggests a mismatch with reductionist ontologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that reductionist ontological naturalism is implausible given actual mathematical methodology and practice; Kitcher and Mill responses/modifications are discussed, but the objection remains influential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological objection to platonism (Benacerraf problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If mathematical entities are abstract and causally isolated, we lack a satisfactory account of how we could know or form reliable beliefs about them; this epistemological difficulty motivates ontological naturalism allied with epistemological naturalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benacerraf (1973) and related literature argue that causal isolation undermines knowledge of abstracta; responses include various forms of naturalising epistemology or revising ontology (nominalism, reductionism), but the problem is central to debates over mathematical ontology and epistemology.
